title: ADAMS v EVEREDGE GLOBAL LIMITED
text:
IN THE EMPLOYMENT RELATIONS AUTHORITY
AUCKLAND
I TE RATONGA AHUMANA TAIMAHI
TᾹMAKI MAKAURAU ROHE
[2026] NZERA 509
3340701
3430524
BETWEEN PAUL ADAMS
Applicant in 3340701
Respondent in 3430524
AND EVEREDGE GLOBAL
LIMITED
Respondent in 3340701
Applicant in 3430524
Member of Authority: Nicola Craig
Representatives: Scott Worthy, counsel for Paul Adams
Michael O’Brien, counsel for EverEdge Global Ltd
Investigation Meeting: 7 and 8 April 2026 in Auckland and by audiovisual link
Submissions (and further 14 and 28 April 2026 from Mr Adams
information) received: 21 April 2026 from EverEdge Global Ltd
Determination: 29 July 2026
DETERMINATION OF THE AUTHORITY
Employment relationship problem
[1] Paul Adams founded the EverEdge business in 2013.
[2] EverEdge Global Ltd (EverEdge or the company) is a specialist advisory firm that
advises companies on how to identify, protect, value and commercialise intangible assets
such as patents, data, brands and know-how. Mr Adams was the company’s CEO until
May 2024 as well as a director of the company until he resigned from that role on 14
March 2024.

[3] Mr Adams was also an EverEdge shareholder through his family trust, the Arrakis
Trust, of which he is the sole director.
[4] In September 2023 the Arrakis Trust and the other EverEdge director/shareholder
Tyler Capson entered into an agreement to sell some of their EverEdge shares with a
Singaporean company Meyzer360Holdings Pte Ltd (Meyzer). Meyzer is controlled by
Singaporean resident Way Siong (also known as Max) Goh.
[5] Things did not go smoothly in the implementation of the sale and purchase
agreement (SPA). Meanwhile Mr Adams moved to Amsterdam intending to continue as
CEO, he says with EverEdge’s and Mr Goh’s agreement. Almost two months later the
company stopped paying him and after three fortnightly pay cycles with no payments
received, he resigned.
[6] Mr Adams brings disadvantage and constructive dismissal grievances to the
Authority.1 EverEdge does not accept Mr Adams’ claims and initially counterclaimed,
pursuing damages due to alleged breaches of Mr Adams’ contractual and statutory duties.2
The Authority’s investigation
[7] An investigation meeting was set in Auckland to hear evidence over three days, 7
to 9 April 2026. As Mr Adams’ representative pointed out there was little evidence
lodged regarding the counterclaim.
[8] At the start of the investigation meeting, prior to any evidence being heard,
EverEdge’s claims were withdrawn. The meeting proceeded to consider Mr Adams’
issues over 7 and 8 April 2026. Evidence was heard under oath or affirmation from Mr
Adams, Mr Capson (former EverEdge director, current shareholder and former COO with
additional CFO functions) and Mr Goh. Mr Capson gave evidence by audio-visual link
from the United States.
[9] This determination has not recorded all material received from the parties but has
stated findings, expressed conclusions and specified orders made as a result, as permitted
by s 174E of the Employment Relations Act 2000 (the Act).
1 File 3340701.
2 File 3430524.

Issues
[10] The issues for investigation are:
(a) Did EverEdge act unjustifiably to Mr Adams’ disadvantage regarding a
failure to pay his salary from 15 March 2024 until the date of resignation?
(b) Was Mr Adams constructively dismissed and if so, was that unjustifiable?
(c) Did EverEdge breach its:
• Duty of good faith
• Duty under s 4 of the Wages Protection Ac 1983 to pay the entire
amount of wages without deduction
• Contractual obligation to pay Mr Adams?
(d) If a grievance and/or breach of those obligations is established, and
considering any contribution, should Mr Adams receive:
• Payment of unpaid salary
• Payment of notice period
• Lost remuneration from his dismissal until at least 31 March
2026
• Compensation for humiliation, loss of dignity and injury to
feelings
• Penalties for statutory (good faith and Wages Protection Act) and
contractual (obligation to pay) breaches?
(e) Should either party have to contribute to the costs of the other?
Events before Meyzer’s involvement
[11] Having been the founder of EverEdge, Mr Adams is employed as CEO on a signed
2014 individual employment agreement (the 2014 agreement). That agreement included
his place of work as Takapuna with the ability of EverEdge to relocate Mr Adams to
another location in Auckland.
[12] There are some changes of directors and shareholders prior to Meyzer’s
involvement. By March 2023 Mr Adams and Mr Capson are the sole EverEdge directors.
Mr Capson was based in New Zealand for some time then moved to be based int eh United
States, still employed by EverEdge.
The SPA
[13] Meyzer, Mr Capson and the Arrakis Trust sign the share purchase agreement on
7 September 2023. One of the terms of the SPA is that an employment agreement will

be executed between EverEdge and Mr Adams requiring him to remain employed until
at least 31 March 2026.
[14] Mr Adams says that multiple obligations of the SPA are breached, including his
trust and Mr Capson not being paid the majority of the consideration promised under the
SPA for his shares. Meyzer and Mr Goh have a different perspective.
Discussions about Mr Adams’ role
[15] In terms of this proceeding, critical events relate primarily to the issue of Mr
Adams’ move, with his family, to Amsterdam in the Netherlands, where his partner is
transfer to a job.
[16] Mr Adams refers to the move to Amsterdam being first raised with Meyzer by
him in August 2023, well before the SPA was signed. Mr Goh acknowledges under
questioning that there were discussions with Meyzer about Mr Adams’ move around this
time although the length of his Amsterdam placement was not finalised. Mr Capson’s
evidence supports Mr Adams’ move to Amsterdam being discussed before the SPA was
signed.
[17] In mid-September 2023 Mr Goh sends Mr Adams a What’s App message with Mr
Goh’s European flight details, where he will be touring and is going to visit Mr Adams
in February 2024 in Amsterdam. Mr Adams describes Meyzer as encouraging his move
as it would promote the business’s European expansion.
[18] I accept that Mr Adams’ relocation to Amsterdam was apparent and known to
Meyzer from August 2023. There is potentially some lack of clarity about how long that
was to be for.
[19] Discussions occur about the nature of Mr Adams’ role and whether there will be
a scope and title shift to ‘Executive Chair’ shift. He is also to take two months’ leave
prior to his start in Amsterdam, with an interim Co-CEOs arrangement implemented,
including one person appointed by Meyzer.
[20] As part of the SPA process, on 15 November 2023 Mr Adams emails the Meyzer
appointee about Mr Adams and Mr Capson’s employment agreements, which Meyzer
want signed pre-SPA completion and which are due for an upgrade. He attaches a
reassignment letter regarding his move to Amsterdam from 1 February 2026 for an

assignment to 31 December 2026 (as per the SPA commitment), noting its needed
regarding a Dutch tax arrangement. Also attached is a draft employment agreement,
based on EverEdge’s standards template with other changes as required by the SPA.
[21] Mr Adams repeatedly requested that Meyzer signed the employment agreement.
It provided little or no response on the specifics of the proposed agreement. Mr Adams
and Mr Capson see this as representative of Meyzer and Mr Goh’s approach of being non-
communicative on significant matters, with approval of their employment agreements
being used as a Meyzer bargaining tool for the deteriorating relationship with the Arrakis
Trust and Mr Capson. There is evidence in an open offer with the employment situation
being caught up in resolution attempts of wider SPA issues.
[22] Mr Adams follows up but becomes very concerned about his need for a written
employment agreement in order to meet immigration requirements.
[23] Ultimately, he asks Mr Capson, as EverEdge director, to sign off the assignment
letter and employment agreement. Mr Capson signs the letter on 1 January 2024.
Mr Adams relocates to Amsterdam
[24] With his family, Mr Adams moves to Amsterdam, seeing his employment there
being effective 1 February 2024. He had been on leave for a period before that point,
although he is still undertaking company communications.
[25] On 4 February 2024 Mr Capson, as EverEdge director, approved a new
employment agreement for Mr Adams on Mr Adams’ request. It specified that Mr Adams
would be:
i) employed on a fixed term ending on 31 December 2026 - clause 2.1
ii) for the period 1 February 2024 (onwards) he would be based in Amsterdam
– Appendix A.
[26] That fixed term was based on the time period to the end of 2026 which Mr Adams
was required to commit himself to EverEdge as part of the SPA.
[27] The 2024 employment agreement is not provided to Meyzer or Mr Goh during the
time of Mr Adams’ employment with EverEdge.

[28] Control of EverEdge is vested in Meyzer on 12 February 2024. Mr Goh becomes
an EverEdge director on 19 February 2024 and shortly thereafter, other Meyzer
appointees also join the board.
[29] Mr Goh is aware of Mr Adams’ move. He communicated on 15 February 2024
that there would be a reshaped culture so Mr Adams “can continue to be in Amsterdam
and CEO at the same time sustainably”. EverEdge continues to pay Mr Adams his salary
in New Zealand dollars into his bank account here, after New Zealand PAYE is deducted.
[30] Mr Adams describes the relationship between him as EverEdge director and via
his trust, shareholder, and Meyzer as deteriorating. He puts this down to Meyzer’s failure
to follow its obligations. Mr Adams resigns as EverEdge director by 14 March 2024
letter, concerned about some EverEdge directors not acting in the company’s best
interests and taking actions to block the proper action of the board.
[31] There is no indication in that correspondence of him resigning as CEO as well, in
fact he specifically says he is resigning as director only, and he “remains under his
existing terms and conditions of employment” as CEO.
[32] Mr Adams is paid his salary for the last time on 15 March 2024, with payment
made up to that date. He is usually paid fortnightly in arrears.
EverEdge’s failure to pay salary
[33] EverEdge fails to pay Mr Adams his usual salary on 29 March 2024. This leads
to him repeatedly contacting the EverEdge board and Mr Goh about his unpaid salary:
• 1 April 2024 – Mr Adams messages the EverEdge board via What’s App
- “Noticed my pay has not gone through and wondered why that is? Could
someone please explain what is going on?”
• The next day he messages Mr Goh – “Given that I remain as CEO could
someone therefore please explain why I have not been paid as my salary
was meant to be deposited into my bank account on 29/3/24 (two weeks
from the last pay cycle) and no payment has been received”.
• On 3 April 2024 Mr Adams sends another message to the Board asking
why his salary had not been paid and why EverEdge is withholding
payment.

• The following day he informs the Board he has still not been paid and
advises – “Please be aware this is [a] breach of my employment contract
as CEO and NZ law”.
• On 8 April 2024 Mr Adams proceeds to inform the Board by email that
“EverEdge is in breach of the Wages Protection Act 1993 [sic] for failing
to pay my salary on 29/3/24”.
[34] EverEdge continues not to pay on cycles 12 and 26 April 2024. Mr Adams
continues to seek payment. He says he continues to work. No substantive reply is
received from the EverEdge Board, Meyzer or Mr Goh regarding why he is not being
paid.
[35] On 1 May 2024 Mr Adams writes to the Board:
As you are well aware I have not been paid since 15 March 2024. I have repeatedly
warned the Board that this is [a] breach of employment contract as CEO as well as
a breach of the Wages Protection Act 1993 [sic].
I require my entire missed pay back to 15/3/24 to be paid no later than 5pm Paris
time 1/5/24 (today). I have requested this on multiple occasions and there is no
reason payment cannot be made immediately.
[36] No salary is paid. By 1 May 2024 email, Mr Adams resigns his employment,
setting out:
• he has not been paid salary due and owing under his employment
agreement since 15 March 2024 despite repeated requests that his salary
be paid immediately;
• this failure to pay his salary was a fundamental breach of his terms and
conditions of employment; and
• EverEdge’s breach of duty has caused his resignation and he will be
bringing a constructive dismissal claim.
EverEdge’s arguments
[37] Before looking at the constructive dismissal question, I examine two main
arguments from Mr Goh and Meyzer, now representing EverEdge made at the
investigation meeting and in submissions – regarding the 2024 employment agreement
and whether Mr Adams actually worked in Amsterdam. It is fair to say that neither of

these were evidently pursued in EverEdge’s initial responses to Mr Adams’ raising of his
non-payment or in response to his resignation.
The employment agreements
[38] EverEdge and Mr Goh say that they were entitled to rely on the 2014 employment
agreement which had Mr Adams working in Auckland. However, there is not
insubstantial evidence that Meyzer and Mr Goh were aware of and agreeable to Mr
Adams moving to Amsterdam and were working around that. Regardless of whether
Meyzer and Mr Goh were aware of the 2024 agreement they had effectively agreed to Mr
Adams moving to the Netherlands and continuing to work even if they thought it was for
a shorter period than the 2024 agreement specified.
[39] I note working remotely was not a new concept for EverEdge. Mr Capson had
been based in New Zealand for some time then returned to his home country, the United
States and continued to work for EverEdge from there.
[40] EverEdge notes that the 4 February 2024 employment agreement signed by Mr
Adams and Mr Capson was not provided to EverEdge when controlled by Mr Goh, during
Mr Adams’ employment, nor to the Authority or EverEdge when the proceedings are
lodged, being only provided or referred to when Mr Adams’ reply evidence is provided.
[41] Mr Adams disputes this pointing to reference to the letter of assignment and his
new employment agreement in his first witness statement and attachment of both
documents to that first witness statement. He also explains to the Authority that he did
not initially inform Meyzer or Mr Goh of that agreement given it was to be a stopgap
measure while discussions about the SPA implementation continued. In addition, he did
not envisage the new agreement would be relevant on filing as he had no sense that
EverEdge would claim he moved without the company’s knowledge to Amsterdam. Once
it was apparent the new agreement was relevant, he supplied it with his first witness
statement to the Authority.
[42] Any potential breach of the SPA obligations by Mr Adams in terms of the non-
provision of the 2024 agreement to Meyzer, was not expanded on by EverEdge to the
Authority and in any event the Authority’s focus is on the employment relationship.
[43] If EverEdge had considered Mr Adams had moved to the Netherlands to work
without permission, then it should have raised that issue with him for discussion and/or

demanded that he returned to Auckland. It did not do so, rather it just stopped paying
him about two months later without identifying the reason it was doing so.
Mr Adams’ amount of work in Amsterdam
[44] In 2024 EverEdge did not explain its ceasing of payment to Mr Adams as related
to him stopping work on his relocation. But it was one of several rationale offered in
evidence by Mr Goh, referred to in more detail below.
[45] Mr Capson’s position at the time, according to a couple of communications
provided by EverEdge at the time of the investigation meeting, was that he saw Mr Adams
as not attending some meetings which he should have or responding to emails promptly.
By the time of the Authority meeting, after Mr Capson had experienced his own departure
from EverEdge, his evidence was that Mr Adams had continued to function as CEO after
his move to Amsterdam. He did have a somewhat limited view of Mr Adams’ work
performance, being based in a different time zone and country. Mr Capson does note
that, by this point, EverEdge effectively had four global offices – Auckland, Singapore,
the United States and the Netherlands, so Mr Adams could effectively have worked at
any of them.
[46] It was not easy, with the short notice announcement of this argument at the
investigation meeting, to dig deeply into these arguments. No other witnesses were
offered by EverEdge on this issue. However, Mr Adams offered and provided his
Outlook calendars showing a number of EverEdge related meetings. Some appeared more
likely regular, pre-arranged meetings, but others were relating to particular topics which
could well be seen as recently arising. There were many dozen pre-arranged EverEdge
related meetings in his calendar over the period in which he was in Amsterdam. He also
relies on his many emails – he says 1072 emails were sent from his work email address
in the relevant period. Mr Adams also recalls being involved in other tasks and activities
not necessarily evidenced in his calendar or email communications, as is the case with
many jobs.
[47] Mr Adams’ evidence was that he continued to work diligently as CEO, performing
CEO duties – making sales, running internal meetings, administration, overseeing staff
and finance. Mr Adams indirectly remained a significant shareholder in EverEdge,
motivating him to make the new structure successful. For example, when in Amsterdam

he drafted a plan, referred to as Operation Bluebell, outlining the work required, including
by him, during the upcoming weeks and months to restore EverEdge’s finances.
[48] There is certainly enough evidence of some work for EverEdge being undertaken
by Mr Adams from Amsterdam. If there were concerns at the time regarding his level of
performance these should have been raised with him.
Constructive dismissal
[49] Mr Adams says he was constructively dismissed by EverEdge. The company
denies that.
[50] Of the three established categories of constructive dismissal Mr Adams asserts
that he is covered by:
i) a fundamental breach of duty – non-payment of salary; and
ii) alternatively, that EverEdge followed a course of conduct with the
deliberate and dominant purpose of coercing him to resign.3
[51] In the ‘breach of duty’ category, the approach is to examine whether:
i) the resignation was caused by the employer’s breach of duty; and
ii) the breach of duty was of sufficient seriousness to make it reasonably
foreseeable by the employer that the employee would not be prepared to
work under those conditions – was a substantial risk of resignation
reasonably foreseeable?4
[52] For ‘course of conduct’ constructive dismissals acting, without reasonable and
proper cause, in a manner calculated or likely to destroy or seriously damage the
relationship of confidence and trust.5
3 Auckland Shop Employees Union v Woolworths (NZ) Ltd [1985] 2 NZLR 372 at 374.
4 Auckland Electric Power Board v Auckland Provisional District Local Authorities IUOW [1994] 1
ERNZ 168 at 172.
5 Woods v WM Car Services (Petersborough) Ltd [1981] ICR 666 at 670 as cited in Auckland Shop
Employees, above.

Breach of duty
[53] There is little difficulty establishing that employers are prima facie required to
pay employees for performing their work. EverEdge is contractually obligated under both
versions of employment agreement to pay Mr Adams’ salary. Likewise, section 4 of the
Wages Protection Act 1983 requires employers to pay the entire amount of wages
payable, without deduction, when salary becomes payable to the employee.
[54] In the absence of evidence of accidental non-payment, it must be taken that
EverEdge deliberately decided to cease paying Mr Adams, without informing him of that,
or indeed communicating with him when he expressed concern about non-payment.
[55] Having failed to pay initially on 29 March 2024, it continued this practice, again
failing to pay on 12 April and 26 April 2024.
[56] EverEdge now relies on clauses in either the 2014 or 2024 agreements that Mr
Adams agreed to deductions from salary for unauthorised absences from work. It argues
that employees who act in bad faith are not entitled to recover wages that would otherwise
be payable due to their own bad faith – Mana Coach Transport Services Ltd v New
Zealand Tramways and Public Transport Union Inc.6 Employees who acted in bad faith,
misleading or deceiving their employer are said to be not entitled to payment.
[57] As noted above, the assertion regarding inadequate work being undertaken was
raised late but I am satisfied that there is sufficient proof of Mr Adamas undertaking some
work when he was in Amsterdam, so do not see bad faith in that regard.
[58] Despite lack of contemporaneous evidence to that effect, Mr Goh may have felt
Mr Adams was not working, but even if EverEdge was unhappy with Mr Adams’
performance as CEO and/or his move to Amsterdam, this did not entitle it in the
circumstances described above to simply unilaterally stop paying him his salary. It was
entitled to communicate and discuss its concerns with him and investigate but there was
no basis to fail to pay him in the meantime.
[59] In terms of two step constructive dismissal test, Mr Adams’ resignation was
caused by the total absence of salary payment over three paydays. That was a sufficiently
serious breach, including in light of Mr Adams’ April communications about non-
6 Mana Coach Transport Services Ltd v New Zealand Tramways and Public Transport Union Inc [2015]
NZEmpC 44, at 171 – 172.

payment, to make it reasonably foreseeable by the employer that Mr Adams would not be
prepared to continue to work for it under the prevailing condition of not being paid any
salary.
Deliberate and dominant purpose
[60] If I am wrong regarding that assessment I consider whether this category of
constructive dismissal is satisfied.
[61] There was evidence that EverEdge, and in particular Mr Goh, was unhappy with
Mr Adams. Mr Capson’s evidence indicated:
i) Mr Goh was extremely angry at Mr Adams after his resignation as a
director, threatening to fire him as CEO; and
ii) Mr Goh decided to fire Mr Adams, with the person who ran the company’s
operations telling Mr Capson that Mr Goh had instructed him not to pay
Mr Adams’ salary in the last payroll run in March 2024.
[62] Mr Capson said the EverEdge’s board saw that the quickest option, rather than
go through a timely employment process, was to stop paying him. Evidencing this is a 1
May 2024 email, lodged by EverEdge, from Mr Capson to Mr Goh and other board
members saying:
I did not agree to withhold payments to him [Mr Adams] without a formal
settlement or conclusion.
[63] I accept the submission that this supports the EverEdge board, other than Mr
Capson, having made a deliberate decision not to pay Mr Adams. There was also
evidence of another person’s and later Mr Capson’s own pay being stopped, suggesting a
practice of stopping payments to achieve a resignation the employer desired. The most
likely reason for stopping pay in Mr Adams’s situation was to put pressure on him in
respect of ongoing negotiations and settlement discussions regarding the SPA.
[64] EverEdge’s position regarding why it stopped paying Mr Adams was not assisted
by it providing several explanations in the investigating meeting, some for the first time
and some seemingly contradictory to other explanations:

i) Mr Adams resigned his employment on 14 March 2024 when he resigned
as director – an argument made despite, I note, his communication clearly
indicating that his resignation at that time was solely as director;
ii) The EverEdge board decided to only pay junior staff and not seniors – with
no documentary evidence in support of this provided, when seemingly it
be readily supported by payroll records;
iii) Mr Adams had moved to Amsterdam without approval – this is dealt with
above;
iv) Mr Adams was not working when in Amsterdam – also above; and
v) Mr Adams was “contract staff” according to Mr Goh and paid day-to-day
– this “contract staff” concept is not captured in other evidence regarding
Mr Adams’ employment.
[65] The seeming development of some inconsistent explanations, along with the
absence of contemporaneous documentation to support them, does not well found
EverEdge’s assertions. These difficulties along with the evidence to support a desire to
pressure Mr Adams in a manner calculated or likely to destroy or seriously damage the
relationship of trust and confidence, mean it can only be concluded that EverEdge adopted
a course of conduct dominantly and deliberately to coerce him to resign.
Conclusion on constructive dismissal
[66] In conclusion both the asserted grounds of constructive dismissal are made out.
EverEdge constructively dismissed Mr Adams.
Unjustifiable dismissal
[67] Having concluded that Mr Adams was constructively dismissed the question
becomes whether that the employer’s actions were ones which, objectively, a fair and
reasonable employer could have taken in all the circumstances.7 For the reasons
identified above, I conclude it was not. A fair and reasonable employer could not stop
payment completely without raising with the employee and investigating any concerns it
had, and it could not seek to deliberately coerce a resignation through non-payment.
7 The Act, s 103A.

[68] Mr Adams was unjustifiably dismissed by EverEdge.
Disadvantage
[69] Failure to pay his salary was clearly an unjustifiable action by EverEdge, which
was to Mr Adams’ disadvantage. However, given that a dismissal grievance has been
established on the same basis it would be double dipping to award remedies in this regard,
so I take it no further.
Grievance remedies
[70] The unpaid salary prior to Mr Adams’ termination is better dealt with as arrears,
see below. Regarding the unpaid notice claim, neither party gave each other a notice
period, and that is part of the matrix of constructive dismissal facts so no further payment
is made here.
Lost earnings
[71] Mr Adams seeks lost earnings from the date of his resignation on 1 May 2024 to
at least 2026, that being the minimum period the parties agreed that Mr Adams would
continue to work.
[72] First Mr Adams seeks three months of lost remuneration under s 128(2) of the
Act, which must be provided except in very limited circumstances. For the period 1 May
2024 to 1 August 2024 his total loss is $81,250 (gross) based on his annual salary of
$325,000, plus 3 % employer KiwiSaver contributions.
[73] Second Mr Adams asks the Authority to exercise its discretion under s 128(3) of
the Act to award him more than three months’ lost remuneration for the period from 1
August 2024 to 31 March 2026. Reliance is placed on findings by the Court of Appeal
in Sam’s Fukuyama Services Ltd v Zhang that full loss sets the upper limit, but a broad-
brush approach is needed, with a counter factual analysis undertaken, allowing for
contingencies.8
[74] Alternatively, Mr Adams seeks an extension of his lost remuneration payment
until at least November 2024 when he was able to obtain other employment.
8 Sam’s Fukuyama Services Ltd v Zhang [2011] NZCA 608 at [38] – [38].

[75] There are circumstances which justify extending an award beyond the three-
month period – including Mr Adams relocation in reliance on EverEdge and Meyzer’s
indications of approval and his dismissal when he was in an overseas country where he
lacked local professional networks, familiarity with the labour market and language
proficiency. It was not easy for him to find work in these circumstances despite persistent
and extensive attempts by him to do so.
[76] There were however some tensions with Mr Goh and Mr Adams’ continuation in
the company, and in fact the making of a success for EverEdge in the European market,
were not certain. The factors which made it difficult for Mr Adams on becoming
unemployed, seem likely to have impacted on his ability to develop EverEdge’s European
business had he remained in the job and also having a CEO on the other side of the world
from where most staff worked, is not ideal.
[77] I find that a reasonable assessment of Mr Adams’ lost remuneration to be for the
period from 1 May to 1 November 2024. This includes seven fortnightly payments of
$13,541.67 gross plus $406.25 KiwiSaver contribution and a one payment of a week’s
salary of $6,770.84 gross plus KiwiSaver. EverEdge should pay him $182,812.55 gross
lost remuneration and $5,484.38 as the employer’s KiwiSaver contribution, subject to an
assessment of contribution below.
Compensation for humiliation, loss of dignity and injury to feelings
[78] Mr Adams seeks $50,000 compensation, as he suffered a high level and type of
harm.
[79] Mr Adams was hurt, humiliated and distressed by EverEdge’s actions, particularly
withholding his pay for an ongoing period and refusing to either rectify the non-payment
or engage with him, in a deliberate manner to force him to resign.
[80] Being forced to resign from the company he had founded and spent a large amount
of personal effort, professional reputation and emotional energy on, was no doubt very
distressing. He had had a long involvement with the company and its staff, with his
sudden departure giving no opportunity no say goodbye to them. The difficulties of
finding other work caused stress and anxiety, with Mr Adams finding it depressing to be
rejected many times when seeking work.

[81] There was reputational impact on Mr Adams as a senior level employee in a public
facing position being out of the role, including recent reporting in the NBR.
[82] Overall Mr Adams describes the experience as “pretty bloody traumatic”.
[83] To be balanced is the earlier decision to sell a considerable stake in his company.
The state of relations before Mr Adams left for the Netherlands was not entirely rosy and
he was frustrated by not being able to get resolutions of the SPA issues. Not all Mr
Adams’ suffering was due to the dismissal by way of stopping paying his salary.
[84] In addition, his partner was employed in a role which had been the initiating
reason for the family relocating, so presumably financial pressures were less than they
might otherwise have been.
[85] Compensation of $30,000 is a fair figure before consideration of any contribution.
Contribution
[86] This is the point to consider whether remedies should be impacted by any
contribution by Mr Adams, under s 124 of the Act. The question is whether his actions
contributed towards the situation that gave rise to the personal grievance and were
blameworthy. EverEdge argues that a 100% contribution is warranted, with Mr Adams’
withholding of the 2024 employment agreement and actions in bad faith warranting a full
reduction.9
[87] In focus is Mr Adams’ decision to provide himself, with Mr Capson’s
participation, with an employment agreement basing himself in the Netherlands and not
passing that agreement on to Meyzer and/or Mr Goh.
[88] The new agreement was signed on 4 February 2024. Mr Adams and Mr Capson
were the only two directors of EverEdge at this point. Under his employment
relationship, Mr Adams owed a duty of good faith to EverEdge only. The 2024
employment agreement was signed on behalf of EverEdge by Mr Capson, thus the only
two directors of EverEdge at that point were involved. Effectively the EverEdge board
of directors were aware of the agreement, and agreeable to it. The sale of EverEdge shares
9 Relying on Purchase v The Glenview Club Inc Mana Coach Transport Services Ltd v New Zealand
Tramways and Public Transport Union Inc, Employment Court, Auckland 36/01, 31 May 2001, Judge
Travis, King v Taupo Electricity Board, Employment Court, Auckland, AEC 11/98, 27 February 21992,
Judge Travis, Knapp v Locktite Aluminium Specialties Ltd [2015] NZEmpC 71 at [36] and Lawson v New
Zealand Transport Agency [2016] NZEmpC 165.

to Meyzer had not been completed at that point. Mr Capson stayed on the EverEdge
board for many months afterwards, only resigning on 7 November 2024.
[89] On the evidence Mr Adams needed a signed agreement in order to progress his
immigration to the Netherlands. The document replicated the standard EverEdge
employment agreement which had been put to Meyzer for approval under clause 7.2.8 of
the SPA. Agreement had not been forthcoming in what seems to have been a timely
manner under the SPA and when Meyzer weas aware of the timing of Mr Adams’ move.
Also, the content of the agreement had not been rejected by Meyzer and was in a form
created by external lawyers earlier.
[90] Mr Goh was aware of Mr Adams’ move to Amsterdam, was generally accepting
of that arrangement and there was no indication of this being unacceptable to him on
behalf of EverEdge and Meyzer although the length of the move had not been established.
[91] In the difficult circumstances with time pressures Mr Adams’ actions should not
be assessed as blameworthy. He continued to provide work under either the 2014 or 2024
agreements.
[92] In any event, Mr Adams’ actions in arranging for and agreeing to the 2024
agreement, on the basis of the evidence before the Authority, do not have a causal
connection with EverEdge’s decision to stop paying him. Mr Goh and Meyzer did not
know of the agreement in March 2024 but decided to stop paying anyway.
[93] No deduction for contribution is made.
Subsequently discovered misconduct
[94] EverEdge argues that Mr Adams’ withholding of the 2024 employment
agreement constitutes serious misconduct. It relies on the Salt v Fell Court of Appeal
decision.10
[95] The situation here is not similar to that in Salt v Fell. As already covered above,
the employer, and its upcoming controlling shareholder and director, were aware of and
agreeable to Mr Adams’ relocation to the Netherlands. It failed to provide approval for
the proposed agreement in a timely manner, as required, without explanation, although
not rejecting it. I am not persuaded that the action of the EverEdge directors in signing
10 Salt v Fell [2008] NZCA 128 at [42].

of an employment agreement which was needed for the Mr Adams’ migration purposes
should be seen as serious misconduct and warranting a 100% reduction in remedies.
Arrears
[96] Mr Adams was not paid for the period from 16 March to 1 May 2024. This is
claimed as essentially six weeks or three fortnightly payments of $13,541.67 gross plus
KiwiSaver employer contributions of $406.25 gross.
[97] EverEdge is to pay Mr Adams salary of $40,625.01 gross and employer
KiwiSaver contributions of $1,218.75 gross.
Penalty
[98] Mr Adams seeks the maximum penalty of $20,000 for each of EverEdge’s
breaches of his employment agreement, the Wages Proetction Act and its duty of good
faith.
[99] I have considered whether a penalty is warranted regarding the non-payment of
wages fortnightly, which was in breach of his employment agreement and in breach of
the Wages Protection Act. However, these elements were core to Mr Adams’s success in
his constructive dismissal grievance and whilst that may not completely rule out a penalty,
I am not persuaded that one is warranted in these circumstances. Had one been
considered, the agreement and statutory breach are likely to have been considered
globally as one.
[100] I have considered whether a penalty is warranted regarding the failure by
EverEdge to communicate actively and constructively with Mr Adams regarding his
move to Amsterdam and express any concerns it had about this change.
[101] Instead, it communicated relatively positively about the move but may have
subsequently decided that it was not really in favour of his being located in Europe. This
was not properly explored with him. Any concerns about his work level after the move
were not explored with him either. EverEdge was not active and communicative in
responding about why Mr Adams’ pay had been ceased or rectifying that situation.
[102] These difficulties were serious and sustained, with EverEdge not being active and
constructive in its communications with Mr Adams in order to maintain a productive
employment relationship.

[103] In considering the appropriate penalty I assess the mandatory considerations in s
133A of the Act and from decisions.11
[104] Good faith obligations are an important part of an employer’s duties, including in
consideration of the inequality of bargaining powers, referenced in the objects of the
Act.12 These absences of communication went to the heart of the employment
relationship and must be seen as intentional. They were particularly unfortunate when
Mr Adams was away from his previous home base and the EverEdge Auckland office.
[105] The appropriate penalty is $7,500, with is all to be paid to Mr Adams.
Orders
[106] Everedge Global Ltd is ordered to pay Paul Adams within 28 days of the date of
this determination:
i) arrears being salary of $40,625.01 gross and employer KiwiSaver
contributions of $1,218.75 gross;
ii) for his grievance, $182,812.55 gross lost remuneration and $5,484.38 as
employer KiwiSaver contribution, along with compensation for
humiliation, loss of dignity and injury to feelings of $30,000; and
iii) a penalty of $7,500 for breach of its duty of good faith.
Costs
[107] Costs are reserved. The parties are encouraged to resolve any issue of costs
between themselves.
[108] If the parties are unable to resolve costs, and an Authority determination on costs
is needed, Mr Adams may lodge, and then should serve, a memorandum on costs within
28 days of the date of this determination. From the date of service of that memorandum
EverEdge then has 14 days to lodge any reply memorandum. On request by either party,
an extension of time for the parties to continue to negotiate costs between themselves may
be granted.
